One night, around 2am, I was on a pair of snowshoes about 2 miles back in the woods, down a valley on a trail near my house. It wasn't that cold, maybe 0 or 10f and the moon was out meaning I could see a bit beyond my headlamp. I was exploring the valley off the main trail where someone had cleared some land for mining.

The snow up here in winter is very grainy and fine typically. As I moved along on the snowshoes, entire shelves of snow would collapse along with my steps. The sound it made while I was completely alone at 2am in the wilderness is hard to describe. Imagine the sound of the wings from a large bird combined with the hollow hum of a gust of wind. I would make a few steps and then get spooked by the sound of a shelf of snow collapsing as a result of my steps and the wind that kicked up in the otherwise totally still and quiet valley. I was really starting to have thoughts of getting out of there until I saw the snow collapse and the corresponding noise it made directly.

Even knowing what it was, turning off the animal part of your brain that says to bunker down at 2am in the dead of winter is hard.

Well, I'm Australian, so you know this is going to involve an animal trying to kill me. I grew up in the country, and one night my parents and I had come home late from a dinner out. It was Autumn (Fall), so there were a few piles of leaves here and there, but as I was walking towards the back door one of them gave me an uneasy feeling. I called out to Dad, "Turn the light on," and he did. Now, we have these spiders called "mouse spiders" because they have a body the size of a mouse... I shit you not, this pile of leaves was what I can only describe as a "small dog spider".

Now Dad had caught up to me and we were both just standing there staggered, staring at this thing in disbelief. I said, "Kill it." He said, "You fucking kill it." There was no way I was putting my leg near that thing, so I told him to grab a shovel and he sprinted off towards the shed. I grew up on a farm. I've had some terrifying experiences with thunderstorms, (most of the land around us was relatively flat..) but the worst for me happened when I was 9. (Summer 2006) I was with my dad and grandpa at my uncle's house half a mile down a gravel road where they were doing some sort of construction/home improvement, and it was all nice and sunny until maybe 6:00 in the evening. This huge wall cloud came out of NOWHERE and my dad had already gone back home so it was just me and my grandpa with his front-end loader tractor.

I'd rode my bike to my uncle's house, and without even thinking twice, my grandpa took off for home, assuming I'd be right behind him with my bike. By the time I got to the end of my uncle's driveway, it started POURING and lightning was flashing all over the place. The loader my grandpa was driving could get up to about 20MPH, me and my bike could go maybe 7 on a gravel road while it's pouring.. By the time my grandpa gets to our driveway, I still have at least a quarter mile to go and I'm crying like a baby because I was so scared that I was going to get struck by lightning. I had to drive underneath some powerlines that went through one of our fields too. When I got home, I was balling my eyes out and went straight into the house, changed into some dry clothes and then sat alone upstairs for the rest of the night.

Sudden spring sleet/snow storm. I was came out of a canyon into a nasty storm that blew in fast and hard. We're talking probably like less than 8 feet of visibility in front of the vehicle. The road iced over in probably less than 15 minutes, and the crosswinds where easily gusting at over 75 mph. I ended up sitting behind a truck that had partially jack knifed because the visibility was too bad to risk trying to get around. I'm used to winter conditions and was in a small SUV, so I wasn't super worried at this point. Its kinda windy here. I mean we don't really get too worried about unless trucks are blowing over on the highway and trees are getting uprooted. So that's when the wind started blowing so hard the stopped car started sliding sideways on the highway. I sat for a while getting a bit anxious when a sherriff's deputy showed up, presumably on the way to institute a road closure and he stopped and came to the window. Wind was so bad we had to shout at each other from 6 inches apart, face to face. He gave me the okay to go around the truck and make for the nearest town, which under normal circumstances is like a 20-25 minute drive. It took almost 2 hours and I don't think I was able to exceed 10-12mph the whole drive. I basically rode the rumble strip to stay on the pavement. That's probably my most white-knuckle winter driving experience. I ended up having to get a motel room because it didn't let up. The next day the sun came out and melted that shit off before I had even made it half of the rest of the way home. Weather's an asshole sometimes.

.3. Human Action as an Ultimate Given

Since time immemorial men have been eager to know the prime mover, the cause of all being and of all change, the ultimate substance from which everything stems and which is the cause of itself. Science is more modest. It is aware of the limits of the human mind and of the human search for knowledge. It aims at tracing back every phenomenon to its cause. But it realizes that these endeavors must necessarily strike against insurmountable walls. There are phenomena which cannot be analyzed and traced back to other phenomena. They are the ultimate given. The progress of scientific research may succeed in demonstrating that something previously considered as an ultimate given can be reduced to components. But there will always be some irreducible and unanalyzable phenomena, some ultimate given.

Monism teaches that there is but one ultimate substance, dualism that there are two, pluralism that there are many. There is no point quarreling about these problems. Such metaphysical disputes are interminable. The present state of our knowledge does not provide the means to solve them with an answer which every reasonable man must consider satisfactory.

Materialist monism contends that human thoughts and volitions are the product of the operation of bodily organs, the cells of the brain and the nerves. Human thought, will, and action are solely brought about by material processes which one day will be completely explained by the methods of physical and chemical inquiry. This too is a metaphysical hypothesis, although it supporters consider it as an unshakable and undeniable scientific truth.

Various doctrines have been advanced to explain the relation between [p. 18] mind and body. They are mere surmises without any reference to observed facts. All that can be said with certainty is that there are relations between mental and physiological processes. With regard to the nature and operation of this connection we know little if anything.

Concrete value judgments and definite human actions are not open to further analysis. We may fairly assume or believe that they are absolutely dependent upon and conditioned by their causes. But as long as we do not know how external facts--physical and physiological--produce in a human mind definite thoughts and volitions resulting in concrete acts, we have to face an insurmountable methodological dualism. In the present state of our knowledge the fundamental statements of positivism, monism and panphysicalism are mere metaphysical postulates devoid of any scientific foundation and both meaningless and useless for scientific research. Reason and experience show us two separate realms: the external world of physical, chemical, and physiological phenomena and the internal world of thought, feeling, valuation, and purposeful action. No bridge connects--as far as we can see today--these two spheres. Identical external events result sometimes in different human responses, and different external events produce sometimes the same human response. We do not know why.

In the face of this state of affairs we cannot help withholding judgment on the essential statements of monism and materialism. We may or may not believe that the natural sciences will succeed one day in explaining the production of definite ideas, judgments of value, and actions in the same way in which they explain the production of a chemical compound as the necessary and unavoidable outcome of a certain combination of elements. In the meantime we are bound to acquiesce in a methodological dualism.

Human action is one of the agencies bringing about change. It is an element of cosmic activity and becoming. Therefore it is a legitimate object of scientific investigation. As--at least under present conditions--it cannot be traced back to its causes, it must be considered as an ultimate given and must be studied as such.

It is true that the changes brought about by human action are but trifling when compared with the effects of the operation of the great cosmic forces. From the point of view of eternity and the infinite universe man is an infinitesimal speck. But for man human action and its vicissitudes are the real thing. Action is the essence of his nature and existence, his means of preserving his life and raising himself above the level of animals and plants. However perishable and [p. 19] evanescent all human efforts may be, for man and for human science they are of primary importance.
